title: "EVSI from a sample: what a study is worth"
author: "Simon Frost"
format: gfm
engine: julia

## Motivation

The expected value of sample information (EVSI) is what the data of a proposed study are
worth before they are seen.
[Experiments and the value of sample information](../04_experiments_and_evsi/04_experiments_and_evsi.md)
computed it exactly for a finite experiment, a likelihood matrix over a few signals and
states. With draws of continuous parameters and data that can take any value, the EVSI
has to be estimated. `DecisionAnalysis.jl` has three estimators, chosen by how the study
is described:

| study description | method | needs |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `SummaryStatistics(table)` | regression of the payoffs on summaries of simulated data (Strong et al. 2015) | one simulated data set per draw, reduced to a few numbers |
| `ImportanceSampling(loglik)` | reweighting of the draws by the likelihood of simulated data (Menzies 2016) | a log-likelihood |
| `GaussianApproximation(focal; n0, n)` | shrinkage of the fitted conditional means (Jalal and Alarid-Escudero 2018) | the prior effective sample size |

All three return a `VOIEstimate`, with the standard error beside the value.

**All numbers are illustrative.**

## The problem

The pond of newts of the two previous vignettes, with no intervention as the baseline.
[The EVPPI vignette](../12_evppi_methods/12_evppi_methods.md) found that the
transmission rate is the parameter worth learning. Here is a study that would inform it.

**The study.** Before the season, `n` tank trials are run. Each trial houses a few newts
with an infected one and yields one noisy measurement of the log transmission rate,
normally distributed around the true value with standard deviation 1. The study's data
reduce to the mean of the `n` measurements.

```{julia}
using DecisionAnalysis
using Random: Xoshiro, randn
include(joinpath("..", "_common.jl"))
include(joinpath("..", "_toy_pond.jl"))

draws = toy_draws(Xoshiro(13), 600)
draws = merge(draws, (; log_contact=log.(draws.contact)))
belief = SampleBelief(draws)
table = outcomes(ToyPond(), TOY_ACTIONS, belief; replicates=10, seed=2026)
problem = DecisionProblem(table, IndividualsUtility(:alive); baseline=:none)
ceiling = evppi(problem, :log_contact)
voi_table(["EVPPI of the transmission rate (the ceiling for this study)" => ceiling])
```

The model takes its parameters by name and ignores the extra `log_contact` column, which
is there for the study. No study of the transmission rate can be worth more than
learning it exactly.

## Regression on a summary statistic

For every draw, simulate the study once under that draw's parameters and keep its
summary, here the mean of `n` measurements. Then ask what learning the summary is worth.
That is an EVPPI with the summary in place of the parameter, so the same regression
machinery applies.

```{julia}
sigma = 1.0
rng = Xoshiro(2)
summary_of(n) = draws.log_contact .+ sigma / sqrt(n) .* randn(rng, length(belief))
by_regression = [n => evsi(problem, SummaryStatistics((; mean_measurement=summary_of(n))))
                 for n in (2, 5, 10, 20, 50)]
voi_table(["n = $n trials" => e for (n, e) in by_regression])
```

The summary must carry what the data say about the parameter, and there must be few of
them: the built-in regression suits up to about four.

## Importance sampling

When the data do not reduce to a few numbers, a log-likelihood is enough. For each
simulated data set the draws are reweighted by their likelihood, which gives the
posterior expected payoff of every action with no refitting.

`importance_loglikelihoods` builds the matrix from two functions of the model: one that
simulates a data set from a draw, and one that gives the log-likelihood of a data set
under a draw.

```{julia}
function importance_evsi(n)
    study = importance_loglikelihoods((rng, θ) -> θ.log_contact + sigma / sqrt(n) * randn(rng),
                                      (y, θ) -> -n * (y - θ.log_contact)^2 / (2 * sigma^2),
                                      belief; seed=3)
    return evsi(problem, study)
end
by_importance = [n => importance_evsi(n) for n in (2, 5, 10, 20, 50)]
md_table(["trials", "EVSI", "standard error", "from the data sets", "from the draws",
          "median effective sample size", "smallest"],
         [[n, Float64(e.value), e.standard_error, e.details.datasets_standard_error,
           e.details.draws_standard_error, e.details.median_ess, e.details.minimum_ess]
          for (n, e) in by_importance]; digits=3)
```

The two functions above are written by hand. For the common designs the package has
them: a study design is an object, `simulate_study` draws one data set from it as its
sufficient statistics, and `study_loglikelihood` scores a data set under a draw.

```{julia}
tank_trials = NormalStudy(:log_contact; n=5, sd=sigma)
θ = (; log_contact=draws.log_contact[1])
data = simulate_study(Xoshiro(4), tank_trials, θ)
other = (; log_contact=θ.log_contact + 0.5)
by_hand(y, θ) = -5 * (y - θ.log_contact)^2 / (2 * sigma^2)
(data=data,
 loglikelihood_difference=study_loglikelihood(tank_trials, data, θ) -
                          study_loglikelihood(tank_trials, data, other),
 by_hand=by_hand(data.xbar, θ) - by_hand(data.xbar, other))
```

The other designs work in the same way. A `TwoArmBinomialStudy` has two counts, one
for each arm (the probabilities here are made up to show the shape of the data):

```{julia}
simulate_study(Xoshiro(4), TwoArmBinomialStudy(:control, :treated; n=20),
               (; control=0.6, treated=0.4))
```

The effective sample sizes are part of the estimate and are printed with it:

```{julia}
last(by_importance[3])
```

The effective sample size is the diagnostic to watch. The more informative the data,
the fewer draws carry the posterior weight. When it falls to a handful, the "posterior
mean" is the payoff at one or two draws, noise and all, and the estimate drifts upwards
towards the plain EVPI. Here the median is comfortable throughout, while the smallest,
for data sets far in the tail, falls to one or two draws for the larger studies.

The estimate has two sources of Monte Carlo error, and its standard error combines
them. One is the finite number of simulated data sets. The other is the finite number of
draws: each posterior mean is a weighted average over the draws, and its error is
carried through to the estimate by the delta method. The two parts are in the table.
Here there is one data set per draw and the two parts are of similar size, so leaving
either out would understate the error by about a quarter. The combined standard error
is comparable with those of the other two methods. It is a
first-order calculation, so when the effective sample size is small it understates the
error and says nothing about the upward drift.

## The Gaussian approximation

The third method needs no simulated data at all. The conditional means given the focal
parameter are fitted once, as for EVPPI, and shrunk towards their mean by
√(n / (n₀ + n)), which approximates how far a study of size `n` can move them. `n₀` is
the **prior effective sample size**: the number of observations the prior is worth. For
a normal prior with variance τ² and observations with variance σ², n₀ = σ²/τ².

The prior on the log transmission rate is normal with standard deviation 0.7
(see `toy_draws`), so n₀ = 1 / 0.49.

```{julia}
n0 = sigma^2 / 0.7^2
sizes = [1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200]
curve = evsi(problem, GaussianApproximation(:log_contact; n0, n=sizes))
md_table(["trials", "EVSI", "standard error"],
         [[n, Float64(e.value), e.standard_error] for (n, e) in zip(sizes, curve)]; digits=3)
```

One fit gives the whole curve. It rises from zero to the EVPPI of the parameter.

## The three side by side

```{julia}
#| output: asis
plt = Plots.plot(; xlabel="number of tank trials", ylabel="EVSI (newts per pond)", xscale=:log10,
                 title="Three estimates of the value of the study (illustrative)",
                 legend=:bottomright)
Plots.plot!(plt, sizes, [Float64(e.value) for e in curve]; label="Gaussian approximation",
            ribbon=[e.standard_error for e in curve], fillalpha=0.15)
Plots.scatter!(plt, first.(by_regression), [Float64(e.value) for (_, e) in by_regression];
               yerror=[e.standard_error for (_, e) in by_regression],
               label="regression on the summary")
Plots.scatter!(plt, first.(by_importance) .* 1.08, [Float64(e.value) for (_, e) in by_importance];
               yerror=[e.standard_error for (_, e) in by_importance], label="importance sampling",
               markershape=:diamond)
Plots.hline!(plt, [Float64(ceiling.value)]; label="EVPPI of the parameter", linestyle=:dash,
             color=:black)
png_figure(plt)
```

The three agree to within about two standard errors. They are different estimators, so they need not
respect EVSI ≤ EVPPI to the last digit; the definition does, and they do up to Monte
Carlo error.

Which to use (after Kunst et al. 2020):

- a few sufficient summaries: **regression**;
- a likelihood but no small summary: **importance sampling**, watching the effective
  sample size;
- a curve over the sample size from one fit, for a study that measures a parameter more
  or less directly: the **Gaussian approximation**.

## The net benefit of sampling, in newts

A study is worth doing when its value exceeds its cost. There are no monetary costs in
this package. Here the cost is in the same currency as the payoff: each tank trial uses
three newts taken from the wild, which are not returned.

`enbs` is defined **only for additive payoffs**: the cost must be in the payoff's units
and must lower every payoff by the same amount whatever is done and whatever is true.
That holds here if the result serves several ponds and the animals for the trials come
from elsewhere in the population. Suppose the result guides the decision at 25 ponds.

```{julia}
ponds = 25
newts_per_trial = 3
net = [enbs(e; cost=newts_per_trial * n, population=ponds) for (n, e) in zip(sizes, curve)]
md_table(["trials", "EVSI × ponds", "cost (newts)", "net benefit (newts)", "standard error"],
         [[n, ponds * Float64(e.value), newts_per_trial * n, b.value, b.standard_error]
          for (n, e, b) in zip(sizes, curve, net)])
```

```{julia}
shown = findall(<=(20), sizes)      # larger studies lose hundreds of newts
plt = Plots.plot(sizes[shown], [Float64(net[k].value) for k in shown];
                 yerror=[net[k].standard_error for k in shown], marker=:circle,
                 legend=false, xscale=:log10,
                 xticks=(sizes[shown], string.(sizes[shown])), xlabel="tank trials",
                 ylabel="net benefit (newts; bars: ± 1 s.e.)",
                 title="Net benefit of sampling, 25 ponds (illustrative)")
Plots.hline!(plt, [0]; color=:black, linewidth=1)
png_figure(plt)
```

```{julia}
best = argmax([b.value for b in net])
(trials=sizes[best], net_benefit=net[best].value, standard_error=net[best].standard_error)
```

`enbs` multiplied the value by the number of ponds. `population_value` does that
scaling on its own, and can also count a decision that is taken again each year: with
a `horizon` the value accrues over that many years, discounted at `discount`.

```{julia}
five_trials = curve[findfirst(==(5), sizes)]
once = population_value(five_trials; population=ponds)
decade = population_value(five_trials; population=ponds, horizon=10, discount=0.03)
md_table(["EVSI of five trials", "newts", "standard error"],
         [["one pond", Float64(five_trials.value), five_trials.standard_error],
          ["25 ponds, decided once", Float64(once.value), once.standard_error],
          ["25 ponds a year for ten years, discounted at 3% (illustrative)",
           Float64(decade.value), decade.standard_error]])
```

A small study pays for itself and a large one does not: the EVSI curve flattens while
the cost keeps rising. With a single pond no study is worth its newts.

`optimal_design` makes the same comparison in one call, over a list of candidate
studies or, as here, the sample sizes of one study, with the cost a function of the
size:

```{julia}
design = optimal_design(problem, GaussianApproximation(:log_contact; n0, n=sizes);
                        costs=n -> newts_per_trial * n, population=ponds)
(best=design.best, criterion=design.criterion)
```

The best size is picked from estimates, so its net benefit is on average a little
flattering, and sizes whose net benefits differ by less than their standard errors are
not distinguished.

```{julia}
[round(enbs(e; cost=newts_per_trial * n, population=1).value; digits=2)
 for (n, e) in zip(sizes, curve)]
```

## A check against closed forms

In the normal model used as a check in the previous vignette (payoffs 0 and p₁ − p₂,
p₁ ~ N(1, 1), p₂ ~ N(0, 2²)), a study of `m` observations of p₁ with standard deviation
1 has a closed-form EVSI: the preposterior mean of p₁ is normal with variance
m / (m + 1), which gives 0.0723251 for m = 10 and 0.0821176 for m = 100. The prior
effective sample size is 1.

```{julia}
rng = Xoshiro(20261123)
n = 40_000
p1, p2 = 1 .+ randn(rng, n), 2 .* randn(rng, n)
normal = DecisionProblem(PayoffTable(permutedims(hcat(zeros(n), p1 .- p2));
                                     actions=[:reference, :new]),
                         SampleBelief((; p1, p2)); baseline=:reference)
small = DecisionProblem(PayoffTable(normal.payoff.Q[:, 1:3000]; actions=[:reference, :new]),
                        SampleBelief((; p1=p1[1:3000], p2=p2[1:3000])); baseline=:reference)
rows = Pair{String,VOIEstimate}[]
for m in (10, 100)
    xbar = p1 .+ randn(rng, n) ./ sqrt(m)
    push!(rows, "m = $m, regression on the sample mean" => evsi(normal, SummaryStatistics((; xbar))))
    push!(rows, "m = $m, Gaussian approximation" =>
                evsi(normal, GaussianApproximation(:p1; n0=1, n=m)))
    study = importance_loglikelihoods((rng, θ) -> θ.p1 + randn(rng) / sqrt(m),
                                      (x, θ) -> -m * (x - θ.p1)^2 / 2, small.belief;
                                      datasets=800, seed=9)
    push!(rows, "m = $m, importance sampling (3,000 draws)" => evsi(small, study))
end
voi_table(rows; digits=4, truth=[0.0723251, 0.0723251, 0.0723251, 0.0821176, 0.0821176, 0.0821176])
```

## What to take away

- `evsi(problem, study)` estimates the value of a study from a sample. The study object
  fixes the method: `SummaryStatistics`, `ImportanceSampling` or
  `GaussianApproximation`.
- Regression on summaries is EVPPI with the summary in place of the parameter.
- Importance sampling needs only a log-likelihood. Its effective sample size is
  reported with the estimate: when it is small the estimate drifts towards the EVPI.
  Its standard error covers both the simulated data sets and the draws.
- `optimal_design` compares candidate studies or sample sizes by EVSI, or by net benefit
  in animals where payoffs are additive.
- The Gaussian approximation gives a curve over sample size from one fit and the prior
  effective sample size.
- No study of a parameter is worth more than its EVPPI.
- `enbs(estimate; cost, population)` is for additive payoffs only, with the cost in
  animals.
